concepts.name: Map projections and the language of physical maps
concepts.description: Why a round Earth cannot be shown flat without distortion, what a map projection and a cartographer are, how the Mercator and Robinson projections differ, and the colour code of a physical map.
concepts.idea: Every flat map of a round Earth is a compromise, so no single projection can be trusted on its own.
concepts.rule: The Earth is an oblate spheroid -- a nearly spherical shape that bulges at the equator and is slightly flattened at the poles because of its rotation. An orange peel cannot be laid flat without tearing, and for the same reason every map has some distortion. The process of showing the Earth on a flat surface is called a map projection, and a person who draws or produces maps is a cartographer. Some maps show the right shapes of countries but the wrong sizes, others the right sizes but distorted shapes. Every map is a compromise, so to understand the world fairly we must look at multiple projections, not just one. The Mercator Projection preserves shape and direction, which makes it useful for navigation, but it greatly distorts size near the poles. The Robinson Projection is a compromise that balances size and shape distortions and gives a more visually pleasing realistic world map. Projections only let us gauge size, shape, location and distance; professionals use latitude and longitude coordinates, which are more precise. On a physical map blue is water bodies, green is plains, yellow or brown is plateaus, dark brown is high mountains, light yellow is deserts and white is ice and glaciers.
concepts.example: On the Mercator Projection Greenland looks larger than India, but in fact Greenland is smaller.

concepts.name: The oceans: extent, life, currents and trenches
concepts.description: How much of the Earth the ocean covers and holds, the five oceans and their key features, how oceans support life and regulate climate, warm and cold currents, and the trenches of the deep seafloor.
concepts.idea: The ocean is not a flat empty basin but a moving landscape that feeds us oxygen, steadies the climate and shelters life even where no light reaches.
concepts.rule: The ocean is a vast body of saltwater covering about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface, which is why the Earth looks blue from space and early astronauts called it the blue planet. The oceans hold 97 per cent of the Earth's water. They support life from tiny plankton to giant blue whales, and help regulate the climate by absorbing heat, slowly releasing it, and adding moisture to the air, forming clouds and rainfall. The ocean floor is not flat; it has mountains, valleys and plains like the land. Plankton are microscopic organisms that have chlorophyll and use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make food, and they make it possible for the oceans to give us almost half the oxygen we breathe. The five oceans are the Indian, the Pacific, the Arctic, the Atlantic and the Southern. Ocean currents are like giant rivers flowing through the ocean: warm currents bring warm water from the equator toward the poles, cold currents bring cold water from the poles toward the equator, and both affect the climate of coastal areas. The seafloor has very deep V-shaped areas called trenches; the Mariana Trench is the deepest, with near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness.
concepts.example: The Gulf Stream flows north from near the Equator through the Atlantic Ocean towards Western Europe, and its warm water makes places like the United Kingdom warmer than other places at the same latitude.

concepts.name: Coral reefs and the naming of seas, gulfs, bays, straits and canals
concepts.description: What a reef is and why reefs are called the rainforests of the sea, the Great Barrier Reef and the threats to it, and the chapter's classification of seas, gulfs, bays, straits and canals with their examples and their role in trade.
concepts.idea: The sea is named by the shape in which it meets the land, and each shape decides what people can do with it.
concepts.rule: A reef is a ridge found at or near the surface of the ocean, formed either naturally or artificially; natural reefs can be made of rock or built by tiny sea animals called corals. Reefs are among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth and are often called the rainforests of the sea, because they provide food and shelter for about one-quarter of all ocean species, including fish, crabs, turtles and sponges. They face serious threats from human activities such as overfishing, pollution and climate change, which makes their conservation crucial. Coral bleaching occurs due to changes in the chemical composition of ocean waters, largely caused by human actions, and the bleaching and death of coral costs a whole host of sea animals their habitat. The chapter classifies smaller water bodies and waterways as follows: a sea is a large, partly enclosed saltwater area connected to an ocean, such as the Arabian Sea; a gulf is a large inlet of the sea deeply cutting into land, such as the Persian Gulf; a bay is a smaller, broad inlet of the sea, such as the Bay of Bengal; a strait is a narrow channel joining two seas or oceans, such as the Strait of Malacca; and a canal is a man-made channel connecting water bodies, such as the Suez Canal. These formations play an important role in supporting trade and transport, and bays in particular provide safe havens for ports and dockyards, shielding them from the strong winds of the open oceans.
concepts.example: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean and so creates the shortest maritime route from India to Europe.

concepts.name: The world's landforms and the Tibetan Plateau
concepts.description: The chapter's working definitions of mountains, plateaus, plains, deserts and continents, and its first stop on the world tour: the Tibetan Plateau, its formation, size, rivers and the name Third Pole.
concepts.idea: A landform is described by its shape, but it is judged by what it does for the land and the people around it.
concepts.rule: Mountains are landforms much higher than the surrounding landscape, recognised by a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit. A plateau rises from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface, with some sides often steep slopes. Plains have an extensive flat or gently undulating surface, without large hills or deep valleys. Deserts are large and dry expanses with very little precipitation and unique flora and fauna; some are hot, like the Sahara in Africa and the Thar in the northwest of the Indian Subcontinent, and others are cold, like the Gobi in Asia. A continent is a large continuous expanse of land, and the most common count is seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. The Tibetan Plateau, north of the Himalayan Range, is the highest and largest plateau on Earth. It is the result of collisions between the Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates, the same collisions that led to the formation of the Himalayan mountain range. It stretches about 2,500 km from east to west and 1,000 km from north to south, with an average height of over 4,500 metres above sea level. It influences the climate of Asia and is the source of many major rivers, including the Indus, the Brahmaputra and the Yangtze.
concepts.example: Scientists call the Tibetan Plateau and its mountains the Third Pole, because it contains the largest reserves of freshwater outside the polar regions.

concepts.name: Asia: the Gobi Desert, the Eurasian Steppes and the Ural Mountains
concepts.description: What makes a desert, the Gobi in Mongolia, the Eurasian Steppes as a grassland and carbon sink, and the Ural Mountains with their minerals, forests, tundra and permafrost.
concepts.idea: Three very different Asian landscapes -- desert, grassland and ancient mountain -- each hold the climate of the wider world in their own way.
concepts.rule: Deserts are large, extremely dry areas of land with low precipitation, less than 25 cm per year. They are found on every continent and cover about one-fifth of the Earth's land area, and according to the National Geographic Society around one billion people, one-eighth of the world's population, live in them. The Gobi Desert is in Mongolia, with part of it in north China; Mongolia is called the Land of the Eternal Blue Sky because it has about 8 to 9 months of sunny weather, though winter temperatures can drop to minus 30 degrees Celsius. The climate is harsh and vegetation sparse, so herds migrate seasonally to reach pastures supported by underground water supplies. A steppe is a large area of flat unforested grassland with a temperate climate, hot summers, cold winters and moderate, often seasonal rainfall. The Eurasian Steppes spread for over 8,000 km west to east; this grassland is a global carbon sink, absorbing carbon from the air and storing it underground, and the steppes and nearby water bodies serve as resting spots for migratory birds like the Siberian crane. Mountains are formed by tectonic forces, volcanic activity and erosion, and they determine climates, serve as water towers, are biodiversity hotspots and often act as natural boundaries between countries. The Ural Mountains are an ancient range stretching about 2,500 km from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the border of Kazakhstan in the south, forming the natural boundary between Europe and Asia.
concepts.example: A tundra is a treeless, cold plain whose soil, called permafrost, stays frozen most of the time and traps greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane; when global warming melts it, those gases escape and speed up climate change.

questions.a: Sample: The Gobi is already harsh, and its herds depend on sparse pasture and underground water, so any further drying would hurt them; the steppes matter because their loss would remove a global carbon sink. But the chapter's sharpest warning is about the tundra. There the permafrost has been holding carbon dioxide and methane like a freezer, and warming melts it and releases those gases, which warms the planet further. concepts.name: Europe: the European Plain and the Alps
concepts.description: How plains and river valleys are formed and what they give people, the European Plain with its soils, crops, minerals, cities and history of conflict, and the Alps with their vegetation, wildlife, minerals and the rivers they feed.
concepts.idea: A great plain feeds and carries a continent, but the water that makes it fertile comes down from the mountains beside it.
concepts.rule: Plains are vast flatlands formed by sediment deposition and are known for fertile soils that support farming, trade and dense populations. Valleys are carved by rivers and provide fertile soil, water and transport routes that have nurtured some of the world's earliest civilisations; together, plains and river valleys sustain agriculture and foster biodiversity. The European Plain, or Great European Plain, is one of the largest flat lands in the world and covers parts of several countries, with low-lying terrain, gentle rolling hills and several wide river valleys. Its fertile soils make it one of the most productive agricultural regions in the world, growing wheat, barley, rye and potatoes; its rivers have been important for trade and transport; and it has deposits of coal, oil and natural gas. Flat land and a favourable climate supported the growth of major cities such as Moscow, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and Warsaw. It has also been the ground for major battles, with many rulers jostling to take control of it. The Alps are a crescent-shaped range about 1,200 km long, forming a natural barrier in south-central Europe and containing famous peaks such as Mont Blanc. They carry oak and beech forests at lower altitudes, spruce and pine higher up and alpine flowers such as the edelweiss in the high mountains, and they shelter ibex, chamois, marmots, golden eagles, lynxes, wolves and brown bears.
concepts.example: The Alps provide water to major European rivers like the Rhine and the tributaries of the Danube, which supply drinking water, irrigation and hydroelectric power to lowland Europe.

concepts.name: Africa: the Sahara, the savannah and the Nile
concepts.description: The Sahara as the world's largest hot desert and the adaptations of its plants, animals and people, the tropical grassland of the savannah and its wildlife, and the Nile as the longest river in the world and the cradle of ancient Egypt.
concepts.idea: Across one continent, how much water arrives and when it arrives decides everything that grows, moves and settles there.
concepts.rule: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world. Temperatures range widely across it, from 30 degrees Celsius to 46 degrees Celsius, with rainfall below 25 cm and hardly any vegetation, and its flora and fauna have adapted to heat sometimes upward of 50 degrees Celsius. An oasis is an area with water and vegetation in the otherwise dry desert. The Sahara has been home to nomadic tribes who herd sheep, goats and camels and engage in trade, and ancient trade routes passed through it carrying gold, salt and ideas to the Mediterranean world. The savannah is a tropical grassland ecosystem with wide open spaces, scattered trees and seasonal rainfall; it lies mainly between tropical rainforests and deserts, the most famous one being in Africa. It supports elephants, lions, zebras and giraffes, which depend on its grasses and waterholes, and its distinct wet and dry season influences plant growth and animal migration patterns. Human activities such as farming, deforestation and climate change are threatening the balance of these vital ecosystems. The Nile is the longest river in the world, almost 6,650 km long, and the Nile and its basin have been the cradle of the ancient Egyptian civilisation.
concepts.example: For thousands of years the Nile's irrigation has transformed dry lands into fertile agricultural areas supporting wheat, barley, flax, fruits and vegetables, besides giving drinking water, fishing, hydroelectric power and a transport route.

concepts.name: South America: the Andes, the Amazon and the Atacama
concepts.description: The Andes as the continent's largest range, its freshwater, biodiversity and mineral reserves, the Amazon river and rainforest with the communities that conserve it, and the Atacama Desert with its clear skies and its clothing waste.
concepts.idea: One continent holds the world's largest river by volume and one of its driest deserts, and human choices are changing both.
concepts.rule: On the west coast of South America are the Andes Mountains, the largest mountain range in the continent. They are home to Mount Aconcagua, the highest peak in the Western Hemisphere, and to Bolivia's Uyuni Salt Flats, the largest salt flat on Earth; a salt flat is an area of flat land covered with a layer of salt. The Andes are a vital source of freshwater for millions of people, feeding major rivers including the Amazon, the world's largest river by volume. They are rich in biodiversity, home to thousands of species of mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles and fish, many unique to the region, but only about one-fourth of the original flora and fauna remains, which makes them a critical conservation hotspot -- an area where efforts are made to save the native flora and fauna lost generally due to human activities. They also hold vast reserves of copper, zinc, silver and lithium. The Amazon River is the longest in South America, flowing from the Andes in Peru east towards the Atlantic Ocean, and its basin with all its tributaries supports the Amazon Rainforest, an area of tall, mostly evergreen trees receiving a high amount of rainfall. Almost 400 indigenous communities live in the forest and play an important role in conserving it, and the forest is threatened by deforestation and climate change. The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth, stretching about 1,000 km, with temperatures from 40 degrees Celsius by day to 5 degrees Celsius at night.

Resources: vast reserves of copper, zinc, silver and lithium

questions.q: A country in the Andes is offered a large sum to open new mines. Using only this chapter, set out what it stands to gain and what it would have to weigh against that.
questions.a: Sample: The gain is real: the Andes are among the most resource-rich regions in the world, holding vast reserves of copper, zinc, silver and lithium, so the minerals are there to be had. Against that stands what has already been lost. Only about one-fourth of the original flora and fauna remains, which is why the chapter calls the range a critical conservation hotspot, and its own definition of that term blames the loss on human activities. And the stake is wider than the country's borders, because the Andes are a vital source of freshwater for millions of people and feed the Amazon, the world's largest river by volume, so harm done in the mountains travels downstream to people who were never asked.
s: States the gain: vast reserves of copper, zinc, silver and lithium
States the cost: only one-fourth of original flora and fauna remains, a conservation hotspot
Notes the wider stake: freshwater for millions and the rivers the Andes feed

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter puts the Atacama's famously clear night skies and its dumps of discarded clothing on the same page.
questions.a: Sample: Both come from the same single fact, that the Atacama is one of the driest places on Earth. Dry air means clear air, which is why it offers some of the clearest night skies and why its rocky, Mars-like ground has been used by NASA to test rovers. But dryness also means that nothing rots and nothing is washed away, so whatever is dumped there simply stays, and the desert has become one of the world's fastest-growing dumps for clothes discarded by cheap fast fashion. Setting the two together shows that one natural quality can be a gift and a trap at once, which is why the UN treats the waste as an environmental and social emergency rather than as litter.
s: Traces both to the same cause: the Atacama is one of the driest places on Earth
Explains the gift: clear skies for stargazing and Mars-like ground for testing rovers
Explains the trap: nothing decays, so discarded clothing accumulates, hence the UN's verdict

questions.q: The Amazon Rainforest is called the 'Lungs of the Earth'. Analyse what the chapter's other facts add to that name.
questions.a: Sample: The name already says that the forest breathes for everybody, so its loss would not be South America's alone. What the chapter adds is that these lungs are not self-sufficient. The forest stands on the Amazon basin and all its tributaries, water that begins as freshwater in the Andes; and even its soil is fed from outside, by dust carried the whole way from the Sahara bringing the phosphorous its plants need. It adds, too, that the forest is actively kept: almost 400 indigenous communities live in it and play an important role in conserving it, while deforestation and climate change work the other way. So the name describes a service, and the facts show that the service depends on a chain of other places and on what people decide to do.
s: Explains what the name claims: the forest supplies air for the whole Earth
Shows the forest is not self-contained, using the Andes water and the Sahara dust
Adds the human element: 400 indigenous communities conserving it against deforestation

questions.q: The chapter calls the Andes both one of the most resource-rich regions in the world and a critical conservation hotspot. Judge whether those two descriptions can honestly sit together.
questions.a: Sample: Taken separately each is well supported. The wealth is real -- vast reserves of copper, zinc, silver and lithium. So is the damage -- only about one-fourth of the original flora and fauna remains. The difficulty is that the chapter's own definition of a conservation hotspot names an area where efforts are made to save native flora and fauna lost generally due to human activities, and mining is exactly such an activity. So the two descriptions sit together, but not comfortably: they are not two neutral facts about the same mountains but cause and consequence printed side by side, and reading them that way is what turns a list of minerals into a warning.
s: States the resource case with the named reserves
States the conservation case with the one-fourth figure and the chapter's definition
Reaches a judgement connecting the two as cause and consequence rather than as neutral facts

questions.q: Write the four-line label for a museum case holding a single discarded shirt found in the Atacama Desert. Use only what this chapter states.
questions.a: Sample: 'This shirt was found in the Atacama Desert in Chile, one of the driest places on Earth, a desert stretching about 1,000 km. It was made quickly and cheaply to follow a trend, in a country where the people who sewed it were paid low wages, and thrown away when the trend passed. Because almost nothing decays in air this dry, it will lie here far longer than it was ever worn. The desert is now one of the world's fastest-growing dumps for clothes, and the UN calls this an environmental and social emergency.'
s: Written as a short museum label about the object on display
Uses correct Atacama facts: in Chile, one of the driest places on Earth, about 1,000 km, a fast-growing clothes dump
Explains the cause and the verdict: fast fashion, low wages, discarded on a trend, the UN's emergency

concepts.name: North America and Australia: plateau, mountains, lakes and deserts
concepts.description: The Colorado Plateau and the Grand Canyon, the Rocky Mountains and the Yellowstone restoration, the Appalachians and their communities, the Great Lakes and their troubles, and the deserts of Australia, closing with Antarctica as the largest desert on Earth.
concepts.idea: The last leg of the tour shows landforms that people have mined, settled, damaged and, in one case, deliberately repaired.
concepts.rule: The Colorado Plateau is a large highland region in the southwestern United States stretching across several states, covering over 330,000 square kilometres and renowned for landscapes including the Grand Canyon, which has had about 5 million visitors annually in recent years. It is composed mostly of layers of sedimentary rock slowly uplifted by tectonic forces and shaped by erosion over millions of years, and is rich in coal, oil, natural gas, uranium and copper. The Rocky Mountains stretch over 4,800 km, are rich in copper, gold and silver, and support mining, hydropower generation, tourism and agriculture; they were home to large indigenous communities, Native Americans, till about 300 years ago, who depended on the region's rivers, forests and wildlife and regarded the mountains as sacred, and many of whom now live on reservations. Geysers, such as Old Faithful at Yellowstone National Park, are jets of boiling water and steam caused there by volcanic activity deep beneath the Earth's surface. The Appalachian Mountains are among the oldest ranges in the world; fertile valleys, abundant game and natural travel routes let indigenous communities such as the Cherokee thrive, and the range provides coal, timber and natural gas, with tourism and renewable energy growing. The Great Lakes are a chain of five massive fresh-water lakes vital to North American commerce and industry. A large part of Australia is desert, termed the Great Australian Desert, which includes the Great Victoria Desert.
concepts.example: Yellowstone had lost its ecological balance to overgrazing by elk; wolves were introduced in 1995, the predator reduced the elk population, the flora returned and balance was restored.

questions.q: A national park is losing its plants because one animal has become too numerous. Using the Yellowstone case, describe what was done there and what it shows about ecosystems.
questions.a: Sample: At Yellowstone the same thing had happened: elk, a type of deer, were overgrazing the park and it had fallen into ecological imbalance. What was done was not to remove the elk but to restore what had been missing from the system. In 1995 wolves were introduced, and this predator hunted the elk and brought their numbers down, after which the flora returned and the balance was restored. What it shows is that an ecosystem is a set of relationships rather than a list of species: the problem was never the elk themselves but the absence of anything that checked them, so repairing the relationship repaired the park.
s: Identifies the parallel problem: overgrazing by elk causing ecological imbalance
States the action and its result: wolves introduced in 1995, elk reduced, flora returned
Draws the lesson: the missing piece was a relationship, so restoring it restored the balance

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter says the Appalachians hold spiritual significance for the people there, immediately after listing what the range produces.
questions.a: Sample: The list just before it is entirely economic -- coal, timber and natural gas industries, with tourism and renewable energy named as growing sectors. Setting a sentence about spiritual significance directly after it puts a second kind of value beside the first, and the chapter marks it as a pattern rather than an exception by saying 'like in other traditions', having already told us that the Native Americans of the Rockies regarded those mountains as sacred. The effect is that the reader cannot finish the paragraph believing a mountain range is simply a stock of resources, which is the chapter's steady position and the reason its third Big Question asks how human actions trigger environmental issues.
s: Notes that the preceding list is economic: coal, timber, natural gas, tourism, renewable energy
Explains that the spiritual sentence sets a second kind of value beside it, echoing the Rockies
Concludes that the chapter refuses to let a landform be only a resource, matching its Big Questions

questions.q: The chapter closes its world tour with a box explaining that the largest desert on Earth is Antarctica. Analyse why that is a well-chosen place to end.
questions.a: Sample: It ends by overturning something the reader has been assuming all along. The chapter's own definition made a desert a large, extremely dry area with low precipitation, saying nothing about heat, yet every desert since -- the Gobi aside -- has been pictured as hot sand. The box then produces Antarctica: over 14 million square kilometres, more than four times the area of India, colder even than the Arctic, and a desert by the definition given on page 13. Ending here sends the reader back across the whole tour to check what else was assumed rather than read, which is exactly the habit the chapter has been teaching since the orange peel and the Mercator map.
s: Notes that the chapter's own definition of a desert rests on dryness, not heat
Gives the box's facts: over 14 million square kilometres, four times India, colder than the Arctic
Concludes that it teaches the reader to check assumptions, as the projections section did

questions.q: Across North America and Australia, does this chapter present indigenous communities as part of the landscape or as people displaced from it? Judge this using its evidence.
questions.a: Sample: Both pictures are there. In the Rockies the communities are spoken of in the past tense: they were at home there till about 300 years ago, living off the rivers, forests and wildlife and holding the mountains sacred, and many now live on reservations established for them. In the Appalachians the communities thrived on fertile valleys, abundant game and natural travel routes, and the Cherokee are named as indigenous to the range. In Australia the Spinifex have lived in the desert for over 25,000 years and their culture is being preserved by younger generations. The judgement, then, is that the chapter presents them as belonging to these landscapes throughout, and that what differs between the cases is not the people but whether that belonging was allowed to continue.
s: States the displaced case, using the Rockies and the reservations
States the belonging case, using the Appalachian communities and the Spinifex
Reaches a judgement: belonging is constant, and what varies is whether it was allowed to continue

questions.q: Write the five-line closing paragraph of a travel article about the world tour this chapter takes, naming three places from North America or Australia. Use only what the chapter states.
questions.a: Sample: 'We finished where the land is at its most extreme. On the Colorado Plateau we stood above a canyon cut through rock that tectonic forces lifted and water spent millions of years carving, among the five million who come each year. In the Rockies we watched Old Faithful throw boiling water into the air, and learned that wolves brought back in 1995 had quietly put a whole park back in order. In the Great Australian Desert we met people whose families have read that country for more than 25,000 years, and saw camels that arrived only two centuries ago. The tour ends with a correction: the largest desert on Earth is not sand at all but Antarctica, over four times the size of India.'
s: Written as the closing paragraph of a travel article
Names three places with correct details drawn from the chapter
Ends on a point the chapter itself makes about landforms, people or assumptions
